title: Harvard, Anthropic, and QuEra Use LLMs to Discover Quantum Circuits with Up to 9,100x Lower Resource Costs - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Harvard, Anthropic and QuEra report an evolutionary framework where Claude writes and iterates complete quantum-circuit programs checked by a classical evaluator, cutting T x Q resource costs of eight fault-tolerant subroutines by 4.1x to over 9,100x versus hand-crafted baselines. The search also surfaced reusable design principles and a new reversible divsteps architecture for modular inversion.

themes.theme: LLM-driven evolutionary discovery of quantum circuits

insights.claim: Researchers from Harvard, Anthropic and QuEra built an evolutionary framework in which an LLM (Claude) proposes complete Python programs for fault-tolerant quantum circuits, checked by an independent classical evaluator.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Frontier LLMs are becoming tools for quantum algorithm engineering, linking AI labs to quantum hardware roadmaps.
insights.quote: scientists from Harvard University, Anthropic, and QuEra Computing have introduced an evolutionary AI framework where Large Language Models (LLMs) automatically discover, write, and optimize fault-tolerant quantum circuits
insights.locator: In a research study published on

insights.claim: Unlike conventional optimizers that do local gate-level rewrites on fixed circuit graphs, the framework lets the LLM search across distinct algorithmic families, with candidates verified for exact correctness via the kickmix model and scored by TQ-cost (Toffoli count times peak qubit footprint).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Whole-program search rather than local rewrites is what unlocks order-of-magnitude rather than incremental gains.
insights.quote: Unlike traditional automated circuit optimizers that perform local, gate-level rewrites on fixed circuit graphs

themes.theme: Resource cost reductions versus hand-crafted baselines

insights.claim: Across eight compilation subroutines, LLM-discovered circuits cut space-time resource costs (T x Q) by 4.1x to over 9,100x relative to hand-crafted baselines.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Lower resource costs for core primitives pull forward the timeline for useful fault-tolerant quantum computation.
insights.quote: reduces the space-time resource costs (T × Q-cost) of core computational primitives by 4.1x to over 9,100x relative to hand-crafted baselines

insights.claim: For the Hermitian code DQI decoder, the AI replaced raw null-space matrix storage with an in-place Lanczos recurrence and striped phase scan, cutting peak qubits from 190,000 to 2,395 and Toffolis from 100 million to 930,000, a more than 9,100x gain.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shrinking a 190,000-qubit requirement to a few thousand moves an algorithm much closer to plausible hardware scale.
insights.quote: dropping the peak qubit count from 190,000 to 2,395 and Toffolis from 100 million to 930,000

insights.claim: For numerical functions used in HHL angle evaluation, Coulomb potentials and Gaussian basis functions, replacing wide fixed-point multiplications with dyadic power-of-two aligned lookups and direct accumulator updates reduced TQ-costs by 9.9x to 39x.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cheaper arithmetic primitives benefit chemistry and linear-algebra applications broadly.

insights.claim: Smaller but material gains were reported elsewhere: 12x for a Reed-Solomon DQI decoder, 7.7x for non-Abelian lattice-gauge simulation and 4.1x for an Fe2S2 alias-select chemistry routine.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Even the weakest results are multi-fold improvements, suggesting the approach generalizes across application domains.
insights.locator: Resource Improvements Across Eight Compilation Subroutines

insights.claim: The evolutionary search repeatedly found that routing data via cheap controlled SWAP gates through one shared uncontrolled arithmetic block beats building separate conditional arithmetic for every branch.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: AI-discovered design rules can be transferred by human engineers to other circuits, compounding the value beyond single results.
insights.quote: Replacing separate, expensive conditional arithmetic blocks for every execution branch with inexpensive controlled SWAP gates

insights.claim: Sizing history stacks and loop bounds for typical rather than worst-case inputs, and accepting a controlled failure rate of about 10^-4, saves hundreds of ancilla qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Trading tiny failure probabilities for qubit savings is a practical lever for fitting algorithms on near-term fault-tolerant machines.
insights.quote: permitting a controlled failure rate (ε ~ 10-4) to save hundreds of ancilla qubits
insights.locator: Bounded Resource Allocation via Failure Budgets

insights.claim: For prime-field modular inversion, the framework found a new reversible architecture for divsteps, a constant-time classical algorithm previously considered unusable on quantum computers due to history storage overhead; a 2-adic invariant lets it decode 87.6% of ambiguous branch decisions and store only 12.4% on a 60-qubit stack.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cheaper quantum modular inversion matters for cryptography-relevant quantum algorithms and thus for timelines of cryptographic risk.
insights.quote: the circuit decodes 87.6% of ambiguous branch decisions directly from the updated registers, storing only 12.4% on a small 60-qubit stack
